To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the genetic and/or antibody-mediated reprogramming NK cells in vivo can be achieved without breaking self-tolerant mechanisms.
the genetic and antibody-mediated reprogrammings of NK cell missing-self recognition are compatible and can be used in vivo for the treatment of cancer.

(i) NK cell education is not required for the killing of HMC class I+ tumor cells, (ii) the blockade of the KIR2DL2/3-HLA-C inhibitory receptor axis in vivo is a promising therapeutic strategy to kill tumors in the absence of self-tolerance, and (iii) NK cell education and self-tolerance can be maintained in vivo after anti-KIR mAbs long-term infusion.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of new strategies for the use of NK cells in the treatment of cancer.
understanding the molecular mechanisms of NK cell recognition and education and how this knowledge can be exploited to develop novel immunotherapy approaches for the treatment of cancer.
understanding the role of inhibitory receptors on NK cells in cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of anti-KIR2DL3 mAbs in the treatment of cancer patients could be beneficial.
the use of anti-KIR2DL3 mAb in vivo reprogrammed NK cells to control mouse syngenic tumor development.
the anti-KIR mAbs can induce a reprogramming of NK cell missing-self recognition, without breaking NK cell self-tolerance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
NK cells are not only able to recognize MHC-deficient tumor cells but also to control the development and the growth of syngenic tumors expressing self-MHC class-I molecules.
NK cells can be reprogrammed in vivo to control tumor growth and that anti-inhibitory receptor mAb can be administered safely in patients.
NK cells can be reprogrammed in vivo and that the use of mAb against inhibitory receptors is a promising strategy for cancer immunotherapy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
NK cell education can be bypassed by using anti-KIR mAbs, which allows the use of these molecules in the clinic without the risk to induce autoimmunity.
the use of anti-KIR2DL3 antibody to block the inhibitory receptor KIR2DL2/3 on NK cells can be used to treat cancer in the absence of the need for HLA matching.
NK cells can be educated by a single inhibitory receptor in the absence of the other receptors.
